title: The Project With CPI 0.75, Not 1.33
subject: civil

presentation.challenge: Actual cost was divided by earned value, producing 1.33 and a false impression of good performance. CPI is EV/AC, so the project was only at 0.75.

practice.primary_question: How are CPI, SPI, cost variance, schedule variance, and EAC calculated from earned-value data?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Reversing CPI as AC/EV instead of EV/AC.

case_dna.target_misconception: A cost performance index above one is obtained by dividing actual cost by earned value.
case_dna.why_plausible: Both values are project cost measures, and the ratio direction is easy to reverse.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With EV=$210k and AC=$280k, CPI=210/280=0.75, showing cost inefficiency.
case_dna.corrected_model: Use CPI=EV/AC, SPI=EV/PV, CV=EV-AC, and SV=EV-PV.

problem_statement: A project has BAC=$500,000, planned value PV=$240,000, earned value EV=$210,000, and actual cost AC=$280,000. Determine CPI, SPI, CV, SV, and EAC assuming current cost efficiency continues.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The performance ratio was inverted.
gates.prompt: Which value belongs in the numerator of CPI?

options.label: CPI=EV/AC and SPI=EV/PV
options.reason: These compare earned progress against cost spent and planned progress.

options.label: CPI=AC/EV
options.reason: That reverses the standard cost-efficiency ratio.

options.label: SPI=PV/AC
options.reason: Schedule performance compares EV with PV, not cost.

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Resolve cost and schedule performance
gates.running_label: COMPARING EARNED VALUE TO ACTUAL COST…

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove CPI and SPI
gates.hint: EV is the numerator for both indices.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The project is both over budget and behind schedule

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the project-control note
report: C3. CPI=280/210=1.33, so cost performance is favorable.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: CPI is reversed; standard CPI is EV/AC.

options.label: EAC=$375,000
options.reason: That multiplies BAC by CPI instead of dividing.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply earned value again
gates.prompt: If EV=$180k, AC=$200k, and PV=$225k, what are CPI and SPI?
gates.explanation: Values below one indicate unfavorable cost or schedule efficiency.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the earned-value analysis
gates.confirmation: I confirm that CPI=EV/AC and SPI=EV/PV, with variances computed as EV minus the comparison value.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Earned value is the numerator in both CPI and SPI.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use standard EVM ratios and variance sign conventions.

seo.seo_title: Earned Value CPI and SPI | FE Civil E-108
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Civil E-108: with EV=$210k, AC=$280k, and PV=$240k, CPI=0.75 and SPI=0.875, not CPI=1.33.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Civil earned value CPI SPI
seo.excerpt: Reversing the earned-value ratios can turn poor project performance into an apparently favorable result.
seo.direct_answer: CPI=EV/AC=210/280=0.75. SPI=EV/PV=210/240=0.875. CV=-$70,000, SV=-$30,000, and EAC≈$666,667 if current CPI continues.

faqs.a: The project is earning less value per dollar spent than planned.
